claims.text: Controlled precipitation aging can induce nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti-type precipitates in a Ti-Ni-primary high-entropy alloy.
The precipitation-aged alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the same alloy in its untreated as-cast state.
The proposed alloy composition is Ti35Ni35Nb10Mo10Cr10 in atomic percent.
The proposed composition satisfies the stated 5–35 at.% per-element HEA constraint and makes Ti and Ni the joint dominant constituents.
Ti35Ni35Nb10Mo10Cr10 forms a single-phase solid solution in the as-cast state.
Aging at about 800 °C will cause Ni3Ti-type precipitates to nucleate and grow in the proposed alloy.
Using an inert atmosphere during aging will avoid oxidation.
Aging between 750 and 850 °C with a suitably tuned duration can produce a fine, uniform precipitate dispersion.
Finely dispersed coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperature.
Impeded dislocation motion increases yield strength and delays plastic deformation.
The aging treatment may increase elevated-temperature yield strength by approximately 10–30%.
The strength improvement will occur while adequate ductility is retained.
The predicted improvement is scoped to mechanical testing at approximately 700–1200 °C.
The exact precipitate phase, optimal aging temperature and duration, and magnitude of strengthening remain uncertain.
Nb, Mo, and Cr may alter precipitation kinetics and elevated-temperature deformation behavior.
A statistically significant yield-strength increase of less than 10% relative to the as-cast control would falsify the stated hypothesis.
Failure to identify nanoscale precipitates after aging would falsify the stated intervention-to-structure prediction.
